assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene followed by experimental discovery of correlated-insulator and superconducting states opened twistronics. A clear, original, high-impact discovery and a new materials platform whose interfaces I can judge from a materials and imaging perspective.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery. The three-person configuration is clean. Other contributors (e.g. Cao, Fatemi and co-authors, Dean, Yacoby, Young and others) are not in the credited list; I note this but cannot expand it.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced by many groups worldwide, with well-defined phenomenology, though the microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated. Eight years after discovery recognition is timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Sample-to-sample variability (twist-angle disorder, strain) complicates interpretation.
Whether the other early experimental contributors deserve credit is not resolvable from the longlist.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators established that band topology gives protected boundary states in real materials: prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect, its observation in HgTe, and observation of three-dimensional topological insulators. Conceptually deep and widely influential across condensed matter, spintronics and quantum materials.
assessment.attribution: Kane (theory, with Mele), Molenkamp (HgTe quantum spin Hall experiment) and Hasan (3D topological insulator spectroscopy) give a defensible three-person split, though Mele, and theorists of the HgTe proposal not on the list, are left out and some parts of the credit are contested.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of independent confirmation, including ARPES and transport; the field is mature and stable. Recognition could be considered overdue.
uncertainties: Credit allocation between Kane-Mele, the HgTe theory proposal and the 3D experiments is unresolved.
The overlapping candidate B025 shows the discovery may need splitting between topological insulators and quantum anomalous Hall effect.
Dependent on my own recollection of priority questions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics gave a controllable architecture for coupling superconducting qubits to resonators and underlies readout, gates and scalable superconducting quantum processors. It is an invention with large, lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Blais (theory proposal), Wallraff and Schoelkopf (first experiments and the strong-coupling demonstration) form a natural trio. Contributions of related groups (e.g. Devoret, Nakamura) are partly recognised through other work.
assessment.maturity: Mature, repeatedly confirmed and widely deployed. The recent prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes timing sensitive: a close follow-on to a prior recognition may be seen as either natural or redundant.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier superconducting-circuit prize.
Boundary between this discovery and general superconducting-qubit engineering is not sharp.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reached fractional uncertainties of order 1e-18 and opened tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. A precise, well-defined invention.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first realised the lattice-clock concept; Ye's group drove the strontium clock to the best accuracy and stability. A two-person split is clean, though others (e.g. Lemonde, Derevianko) have claims to specific ideas and the credit to trapped-ion clock pioneers is already recognised separately.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature; multiple independent clocks agree at the 1e-18 level. Recognition is timely, with the redefinition of the second pending.
uncertainties: Overlap with Jun Ye's other candidate (B014) and with earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock recognition.
Priority for the magic-wavelength concept may be shared.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The qPlus sensor and its CO-tip functionalisation gave atomic-resolution force microscopy of single molecules, bonds and charge states. From my microscopy background it is a real, concrete instrumental advance with broad use in surface science.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor; Meyer and Gross applied it with CO-terminated tips to resolve molecular structure and bond order. The three-name configuration is defensible.
assessment.maturity: Widely adopted and confirmed by many labs, but a well-defined method advance rather than a fundamental discovery; the prize criteria 'discovery or invention' are met in principle but physics impact is narrower than other candidates, and the field arguably lies between physics and chemistry.
uncertainties: Impact on physics broadly is narrower than for field-opening discoveries.
Contributions of other probe-microscopy groups (e.g. IBM Zurich colleagues beyond those named) may need weighing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, then the giant effect in MgO junctions, enabled read heads and MRAM. A clear, impactful discovery and invention that follows naturally from the earlier giant magnetoresistance prize.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported the first reproducible room-temperature TMR; Yuasa (and Parkin, not on the list) realised the giant coherent-tunnelling effect in MgO. The credited trio is plausible but the MgO part is shared with others outside the list, and I cannot treat that as resolved.
assessment.maturity: Extremely mature, decades of independent confirmation and commercial use. Timing is late rather than early.
uncertainties: Credit for MgO junctions is shared with researchers not in the credited names.
Possible perception as incremental after GMR.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Solid-state femtosecond lasers (Ti:sapphire and SESAM mode locking) made compact ultrafast sources central to attosecond science, spectroscopy and metrology. It is an invention that underpins work I highlighted as Chair in 2023 on opening the door to the world of electrons.
assessment.attribution: Moulton (Ti:sapphire laser medium), Sibbett (Kerr-lens mode locking) and Keller (SESAM) form a plausible trio, but the Kerr-lens work and associated credit are tangled and contested.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature with enormous downstream impact; recognition is late and partly overlaps with the 2018 chirped-pulse amplification prize and 2023 attosecond prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier ultrafast-laser prizes may weaken novelty argument.
Priority split between Kerr-lens and SESAM mode locking is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers deliver femtosecond, coherent hard X-ray pulses and have transformed structural dynamics, imaging and materials science. A major instrument-driven invention.
assessment.attribution: SASE theory and concepts involve several groups (Pellegrini and collaborators, Kondratenko and Saldin, Kim); the credited names may not map neatly onto the decisive contributions and I regard the allocation as the main difficulty. Facility building and experimental teams (e.g. LCLS, FLASH) complicate matters.
assessment.maturity: Mature facilities with independent confirmations in several countries. Recognition is plausible but allocation is unsettled.
uncertainties: Priority between SASE proposers is not clear from the supplied names.
The distinction between an accelerator-physics achievement and a discovery.
